$comment: One row per rule in this repository's contract: what enforces it, what it is currently absorbing, and every breach recorded against it. Kept honest by scripts/contract-ledger.mjs (`npm run contract:ledger:check`, blocking inside check:ci): a rule defined in the sources with no row here fails, and a row claiming a rule that no longer exists fails. Most of the numbers are reporting-rung — they inform what AGENTS.md should say next, they never fail a build. The exception is `ceiling`, below. Breaches are appended by `--record`, fed the JSON a rubric review writes.
$ceiling: A row that measures an EXCEPTION LIST (a SAST allowlist, the names a lint fence waves through) or a RATCHET BASELINE carries `ceiling: { max, reason, comesOffWhen }`, and `--check` fails when the count grows past `max`. Why: both lists are the right shape — narrow, each entry read and accepted — and both are one entry away from being the wrong one, because an exception list that grows a line per inconvenient diff erodes its fence without a build ever going red. A baseline is the same thing counted differently: it is the number of findings a rule is living with rather than fixing, and it is one digit in the script that enforces the rule. `max` is what the list or the baseline holds today, so this is green on arrival (ADR-0007). `comesOffWhen` is the field an exemption list normally never has, and the reason exemptions become permanent. Raising a ceiling is fine and is the point: it is one reviewed line next to the change it pays for.
$floor: The other direction. A row that measures a THRESHOLD inside a gate — `FLOOR = 6.5` in scripts/quality-gate.mjs, `COMPONENT_LOC_LIMIT = 200` in scripts/agent-review.mjs — or a ratchet that counts compliance rather than debt pins it with `floor: { min, reason, risesWhen }`, and `--check` fails when the number drops below `min`. Why: those numbers ARE what the gate calls failure. Lowering one turns a red gate green without changing a single answer the product gives, and nothing in a green build looks any different afterwards. Same rule as a ceiling: move it on purpose, in the diff that needs it, with the sentence next to it.
$breaches: Empty for every row today, and that is a statement about the ledger's age rather than about the rules: recorded breaches start accumulating from the first review run that is folded in with `--record`. The 'Absorbing now' column is NOT empty, because absorbed debt (allowlist entries, ratchet baselines, files already over a limit) is measured live from the files the gates read — so this ledger says something useful on the day it lands.

rules.guidance: AGENTS.md § Conventions that bite — components under 200 LOC
rules.why: a component may not grow past 200 lines; one already over may shrink or stay put

rules.enforcedBy: scripts/agent-review.mjs (Part A, blocking) — the number A1 compares against
rules.why: the line A1 draws; the rule above measures the population over it, this pins the line itself

ceiling.reason: 200 lines, the number AGENTS.md, the rubric and docs/roadmap/component-debt.md all state. A1 is a ratchet on growth, so a component already over the line may sit there — which means raising this constant would not turn anything red anywhere, it would simply stop refusing the next overgrown component. That is the softening this pin refuses.
ceiling.comesOffWhen: It does not rise. It could fall, and a fall is the debt catalogue getting shorter — the pin is one-directional on purpose.

rules.why: a segment-level opt-out un-caches a whole route to serve one dynamic read

rules.enforcedBy: scripts/agent-review.mjs (Part A, blocking; unblocked by an `Ack:` line)

rules.why: a deleted test looks exactly like a test that never existed

rules.enforcedBy: scripts/agent-review.mjs (Part A, blocking; unblocked by an `Ack:` line)
rules.why: this repo holds live ad-platform credentials and keeps a deliberately small dependency list

rules.guidance: AGENTS.md § Conventions that bite — a commit subject names the change, not the session
rules.why: the log is what a future agent bisects; 'fix: Done. Here's what I found' is well-formed and useless
a caller that reaches for a driver has picked a backend and skipped the tenant key

ceiling.reason: Nothing has ever been allowlisted against the store seam: every caller reaches data through a store in src/lib, which is where the tenant key is applied. A ceiling of 0 records that, and makes the first exception a diff somebody argues about rather than a line somebody adds.

rules.why: a route that establishes no caller identity mints a phantom tenant instead of failing

ceiling.reason: Five anonymous routes, and each one's caller genuinely cannot sign in: a merchant-feed robot, a webhook from Meta or a mail forwarder, a signed-out visitor on the marketing site, a scan claimed before the sign-in redirect. None is unguarded — each is behind an unguessable 128-bit token in the path, an HMAC over the raw body, or a durable per-IP daily cap, and none spends AI units.
ceiling.comesOffWhen: An entry comes off when its caller gains a real identity: feed/[token] and twin/inbound/[token] when a machine caller can authenticate as the project rather than by holding a URL; images/upload-ref and sken/claim if the marketing site stops serving the signed-out flow they exist for. A sixth entry is not a variation on these — it is a product decision about anonymity, and it belongs in the diff that raises this number.

rules.guidance: AGENTS.md § Security rules are a gate
rules.why: a server env var read in a client module ships to the browser

ceiling.reason: No client module has ever needed a server env var: the shape that works is a server component reading it and passing a value down, and that shape has always been available. A ceiling of 0 keeps 'just this once' from being a one-line edit — the failure mode here is a secret shipped to a browser, which no reason survives.

rules.guidance: AGENTS.md § Security rules are a gate
rules.why: dynamic code execution in a process holding live advertiser credentials

ceiling.reason: Dynamic code execution has never been needed in a process that holds live advertiser credentials, and a model's output is the input most likely to reach one. A ceiling of 0 is the whole rule.

rules.guidance: AGENTS.md § Security rules are a gate
rules.why: SQL built by interpolation; the two exceptions are table NAMES, which cannot be bound

ceiling.reason: Three statements interpolate a table NAME, which SQLite cannot bind as a parameter. Two of them take the name from a literal array written inline in the same file — a PRAGMA in src/lib/db.ts and the three-table sweep in the leads local store. The third, added when the SAST gate was promoted from continue-on-error to blocking (2026-09-01), is the different claim the line below anticipated: src/lib/projects/orphan-walk.local.ts enumerates tables from sqlite_master rather than from a literal, because walking a per-project table nobody registered is the whole point of the dependent-side orphan walk. Its source is the database's own catalogue, not a request, and the name goes through quoted() — SQLite identifier quoting with doubled quotes. In all three, every caller-supplied value in the statement is bound. The two campaign-store statements that were the fourth and fifth findings are NOT here: they were fixed in the same change, by enumerating the eight complete statements they used to assemble.
ceiling.comesOffWhen: Each entry comes off when its call site stops needing a dynamic table name — the PRAGMA when the schema check is generated per table, the leads sweep when leads live in one table, and the orphan walk when the schema is enumerated through a registry the code owns rather than through sqlite_master. A FOURTH entry is not a variation on these: two of the three are literal-sourced and one is catalogue-sourced, so the next one is either a repeat of a claim already made here (fix it the way the campaign store was fixed) or a new one that belongs in the diff that raises this number.

rules.why: a credential-shaped identifier passed to console survives in the platform's log retention

ceiling.reason: Nothing credential-shaped has ever had to reach console. Vercel's log retention outlives the incident, so an allowlisted entry here is a secret with a retention policy attached — the fix is always to log the identifier's shape rather than its value.

rules.why: a route importing the decrypted BYOM key can return it by accident

ceiling.reason: Zero, as of 2026-09-01: the seam this row's `comesOffWhen` described was built. A second route (POST /api/byom/keys, which stores a key and then tests it) needed the plaintext, which was the signal to move the probe rather than to add a line here. probeStoredByomKey / storeAndProbeByomKey in src/lib/llm/keys/validate.ts take a userId and return a ProbeOutcome, so the decrypted key now exists only inside that module's frame and no module under src/app/api imports it at all.
ceiling.comesOffWhen: It is off. The ceiling stays at 0: a route that needs the plaintext key again means the seam is missing a case, and the fix is to widen the seam's verdict, never to hand a handler the key.

rules.why: TLS verification disabled anywhere in a process that talks to ad platforms

ceiling.reason: TLS verification has never been switched off anywhere in this process, and the processes that talk to Google Ads and Sklik are the ones where it would matter most. A local certificate problem is a local problem — it does not earn an entry that ships.

rules.why: a secret-shaped value behind NEXT_PUBLIC_ is a published secret

ceiling.reason: No secret-shaped value has ever been put behind NEXT_PUBLIC_. There is no reason that makes a published secret acceptable, so this ceiling has nothing to trade against — an entry here means the variable was misnamed or the value should not be in the browser.

rules.why: a key-derived cipher with no explicit IV

ceiling.reason: The one thing encrypted here is a user's BYOM key, and it uses an explicit IV. A key-derived cipher with no IV is never the smaller change — it is a rewrite of stored data waiting to happen, so 0 is the only number that keeps that decision out of a hurried diff.

rules.why: the LLM chokepoint and the store seam, refused in the editor rather than in a diff

ceiling.reason: Three names cross this fence, and they are the same name three times: `geminiAvailable`, `claudeAvailable`, `codexAvailable`. Each is a boolean about whether a provider is CONFIGURED — it cannot be used to make a call, which is the thing the fence exists to route through generateStructured().
ceiling.comesOffWhen: When the three probes are re-exported from src/lib/llm/index.ts. Callers would then import the entry point like everyone else and the fence would need no exception list at all. A fourth entry is not another probe — it would be the first symbol that lets a caller do something with a provider, and that is the fence failing, not the list growing.

rules.why: src/lib owns the drivers, so it relaxes the store half — and keeps the chokepoint half

ceiling.reason: The same three availability probes as `adamant/seams`, restated because ESLint merges `no-restricted-imports` by rule id: a narrower block REPLACES the wider one's options rather than adding to them, so the exception list has to be written twice or the chokepoint half is silently dropped for src/lib.
ceiling.comesOffWhen: Together with the copy in `adamant/seams` — re-export the probes from src/lib/llm/index.ts and both lists go to zero. Until then the two counts must move together; one of them growing alone means the fences have drifted apart.

rules.enforcedBy: eslint.config.mjs (the exception the fence is built around)
rules.why: src/lib/llm is allowed to be the exception it enforces on everyone else

ceiling.reason: One waiver: `no-restricted-imports` is off inside src/lib/llm/**, because that directory is the chokepoint — it is where the clients are constructed and the provider order, BYOM keys, demo fallback, metering and telemetry live. A fence has to exempt its own implementation or it cannot be implemented.
ceiling.comesOffWhen: It does not; this one IS the fence's definition. The ceiling is here so a SECOND directory cannot join it quietly — the whole value of a chokepoint is that there is exactly one place the rule does not apply.

rules.why: the editor-time half of A2

ceiling.reason: This fence has no exception list and never needed one: the shape that works under cacheComponents is a <Suspense> boundary around the dynamic read, which is available on every route. `maxDuration` and `preferredRegion` are not exemptions — they were never restricted, because they are Vercel function settings rather than caching opt-outs.

rules.why: an untagged generateStructured call site has no test and no contract golden
a hand-edited golden passes the drift check by construction; the ledger row is what catches it
how good the output has to be, per operation, and which model it was measured on

ceiling.reason: Nine registry tools carry no baked quality score. Every one of them is a tool that landed with its contract golden and whose quality cells are measured on the next full `npm run llm:quality` bake — a bake costs money and runs across six models, so it is deliberately not run per tool. Nine is what the file holds today; raising it means another tool shipped unbaked, which is a decision rather than a digit.
ceiling.comesOffWhen: The next full bake: every tool in the registry gets a cell, and this drops to 0. It has never legitimately gone up except by a tool landing, so a raise that is not accompanied by a new `// llm-tool:` tag in the same diff is a finding being absorbed.

rules.why: a baked score still on the public scorecard for an operation the registry no longer has

ceiling.reason: One: `lead-reply`, retired when the twin absorbed it, whose score is still on the public scorecard. A stale cell is a published number about something the product no longer does, so one is already one more than the right answer — it is here because removing it means re-baking.
ceiling.comesOffWhen: The next full bake, which drops the retired cell. A second entry means a second operation was removed without the scorecard following, which is the drift this counts.

rules.why: a baked serving-model cell with no recorded baseline is a score nothing can be compared against

ceiling.reason: Zero, and it should stay zero: a freshly baked operation has just been measured, so there is no reason not to record what it scored. `npm run llm:quality:baseline -- --reason "…"` records every cell in a bake at once, which makes any non-zero number here a step somebody skipped rather than a cost somebody could not pay.

rules.enforcedBy: scripts/quality-gate.mjs (blocking inside check:ci) — the number the gate calls failure
rules.why: below this score the judge is no longer splitting hairs — it is writing up invented figures

floor.reason: Both serving columns sit at 7.0 or above on every baked operation, so 6.5 leaves half a point of run-to-run variance and still fails a real drop. It is one digit in the file that enforces it, and lowering it would make the gate green without changing a single answer the product gives — which is the whole shape of softening a gate to pass.
floor.risesWhen: After a fresh full matrix shows the serving columns are comfortably higher, per the note above the constant. Raising it is a decision to make on measurement; lowering it is what this floor exists to refuse.

rules.enforcedBy: scripts/flake-drill.mjs (reporting, weekly) + test-unit/flake-census.test.mjs (blocking) + this ledger's ceiling
rules.why: a blocking gate that fails at random teaches people to re-run rather than read a red build

ceiling.reason: Empty, because nothing had ever measured whether these 482 test files agree with themselves — there is no history of flakes to seed it from, and the first weekly run of .github/workflows/flake-watch.yml is what will say. A ceiling of 0 makes the FIRST accepted flake a decision somebody takes on purpose, which is the right shape for the most expensive exception list here: `npm run test:unit` is what stands between a change and master.

rules.guidance: AGENTS.md § The bilingual docs are held in step by a gate
rules.why: the Czech edition going stale is a confident wrong answer, not a gap
a gate must not be able to become a comment by being renamed or made non-blocking
a regenerated instruction block has to be read on its own, not ride along in an unrelated diff
an instruction a generator wrote must be read by a human before it becomes guidance an agent obeys
a settled decision records whether its predicted consequences held
an unset permissions block inherits the repository default token scope

rules.enforcedBy: scripts/actions-pin.mjs — third-party blocking, first-party EXEMPT (STRICT = false)
rules.why: a tag is a mutable pointer; a retagged action runs with the pipeline's token before any downstream proof applies
rules.verdict: green by exemption — the one rule here that passes because it is switched off for the actions this repo actually uses. Closing it is one networked run (`npm run actions:pin`), which no offline session can do.

rules.enforcedBy: scripts/actions-pin.mjs (blocking in CI and check:ci) — the floor SHA-pinned refs may not fall below
rules.why: a pin that nothing enforces comes undone on the next Dependabot bump or copy-pasted step

floor.reason: The one ratchet here that counts COMPLIANCE rather than debt, so it is pinned with a floor rather than a ceiling: it may only rise. It is 0 today because every `uses:` in this repository is first-party and exempt (STRICT = false), which is the exemption `npm run actions:pin` closes in one networked pass — that command resolves every tag to its digest and writes STRICT = true and the new baseline back into the script itself. Be exact about what a floor of 0 buys while the count is 0: nothing yet. It records the DIRECTION before the number moves, so that the raise below is a step somebody takes rather than a convention somebody remembers.
floor.risesWhen: In the same diff as `npm run actions:pin` — that command needs the network, so no offline session can do it, and it prints this as its closing instruction. Raise `min` to the count it reports, and the pin can no longer be undone by a Dependabot bump, a copy-pasted step, or an agent 'simplifying' a 40-character ref back to `@v4`.

rules.guidance: AGENTS.md § Two of these are enforced rather than trusted
rules.why: an expression spliced into a run: body is source code, not an argument
parity is the type system; what typecheck cannot see is measured instead of asserted

ceiling.reason: Thirty-eight hardcoded cs strings still sit outside any T table. The audit cannot be zeroed today, which is why it is on the reporting rung — the baseline is the honest population, and it has only ever moved down (40 → 38 when the /lp variants were retired).
ceiling.comesOffWhen: When the remaining strings move into their component's own T dict and this reaches 0, at which point the audit's coverage half can be promoted to blocking. Every legitimate move so far has been downward; a raise means a new hardcoded string was accepted rather than localised.

rules.why: a cs value byte-identical to its en source is a locale column nobody actually wrote

ceiling.reason: Forty cs values are still byte-identical to their en source, minus the do-not-translate list. This is the count typecheck structurally cannot see: the key exists in both columns, so parity holds and the Czech reader gets English. Forty is what the tree holds; the number has moved down twice and never up.
ceiling.comesOffWhen: As the localization waves transcreate the remaining values. The `RATCHET` comment in scripts/i18n-audit.mjs records that origin/master once measured 44 here — that is exactly the kind of quiet drift a ceiling in a reviewed file makes visible.

rules.why: tykání in the cs column — the product addresses its users formally, and a mixed register reads as a different product

ceiling.reason: Clean today, and the only one of the three i18n counts that is. A register slip is a one-word edit to fix and a one-digit edit to absorb, which is precisely the asymmetry a ceiling of 0 removes.

rules.guidance: AGENTS.md § context-map.json is an index, not an inventory
rules.why: a tracked source file no context maps is a file an agent scoping by context never sees

ceiling.reason: 159 tracked source files that no context in context-map.json claims, measured at the 2026-07-30 scan. The map is honest about being an index rather than an inventory, and this is the size of the gap. It is also the single easiest number in the repository to raise: a scan that maps nothing new still passes if the baseline moves with it.
ceiling.comesOffWhen: As context scans claim the unmapped files. It may only fall — a rise means new source landed outside every context, which is a scoping question for the change that added it, not a baseline question.

rules.enforcedBy: test-unit/mutation-census.test.mjs (blocking inside test:unit) — the floor the number of mutants may not fall below
rules.guidance: AGENTS.md § Coverage says how much code runs + ADR-0007
rules.why: the drill fails on a survivor; nothing failed when the MEASURE itself got smaller

floor.reason: Seven mutants over three seams — cron auth, the spend ceiling and per-IP limiter, and the Sklik write rails — which is what the catalogue holds today. Pinned as a floor rather than a ceiling because it counts COMPLIANCE: widening the measure is the point and may happen freely, while every way it gets worse is downward. Deleting the mutant that started surviving is the cheapest green in this repository — the census still passes and the drill still prints a perfect score, over less of the tree. The per-seam half of the same rule is SEAM_FLOORS in the same file, which stops a level total drifting off the seam that spends money.
floor.risesWhen: Whenever a seam gains a mutant, and whenever a new seam where wrong is a bill or a breach gets one — raise it in that diff. It falls only when a seam genuinely stops existing, and then the sentence in the commit says what now guards what it guarded.

rules.why: the checkout is shared with concurrent agents, so `git add -A` commits someone else's half-finished work
rules.verdict: unfenceable from inside this repo (the damage is done by the time a hook sees it), and it has bitten before — the closest thing to a fence is that a commit which breaks the build is the committer's to fix.

rules.id: never raise a ratchet you could have lowered
rules.enforcedBy: scripts/contract-ledger.mjs (blocking inside check:ci) — every baseline and threshold is pinned above
rules.why: raising a baseline is how a finding gets absorbed instead of fixed
rules.verdict: the candidate fence in this row's previous verdict, built: every ratchet baseline in the repository now carries a `ceiling` here and every gate threshold a `ceiling` or a `floor`, so moving one in its own script is red until the pin moves in the same diff with the reason. What is still judgment, and stays with rubric B3: whether a legitimate-looking reason (a new AI tool shipping unbaked) is the real one, or a regression wearing its clothes.

rules.id: amber work says so in its own words
rules.guidance: AGENTS.md § What you may do unattended — amber
rules.why: a real-model run spends money, so the change should say what it proved and against which model
rules.verdict: unfenced on purpose for now: the reviewable artefact (a commit message sentence) is exactly what rubric A5 already looks at, and adding a second message rule risks making both easier to ignore.

rules.enforcedBy: partly the runtime guards (SKLIK_WRITES_ENABLED, the schranka review gate); the boundary itself is prose
rules.why: spending an advertiser's budget, sending mail, publishing under the operator's name, pushing to master
rules.verdict: the load-bearing half is unfenceable by design — it is about what an agent decides to do, not about what the code allows. Worth re-reading whenever a run reports it 'nearly' did one of these.
